question.text: A $9\,000\,\textrm{mL}$-capacity tank initially holds $6\,000\,\textrm{mL}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $180\,\textrm{g}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $90\,\textrm{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $60\,\textrm{mL/s}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.explanation:
Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} \] describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \]

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{g}/\textrm{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

Step 1: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\textrm{g/mL}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $90\,\textrm{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the salt enters the tank is \begin{align*} \require{cancel} Q'_{\textrm{in}} &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{mL}}\right)\cdot \left(90\,\dfrac{\textrm{mL}}{\textrm{s}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\cancel{\textrm{mL}}}\right)\cdot \left(90\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mL}}}{\textrm{s}}\right)\\[5pt] &= 0\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $6\,000\,\textrm{mL}$ of brine; fresh water enters at $90\,\textrm{mL/s},$ and mixed brine leaves at $60\,\textrm{mL/s}.$ As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ seconds is \[ V(t) = 6\,000 + 90t - 60t = 30(200+t)\,\textrm{mL}. \]

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is \[ \dfrac{Q}{30(200 + t)}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{mL}}. \]

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $60\,\textrm{mL/s},$ salt leaves at a rate of \begin{align*} Q'_{\textrm{out}} &= \left(60\,\dfrac{\textrm{mL}}{\textrm{s}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{30(200+t)} \,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{mL}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(60\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mL}}}{\textrm{s}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{30(200+t)} \,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\cancel{\textrm{mL}}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2Q}{200+t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}. \end{align*}

Step 3: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \\[5pt] &= 0 - \dfrac{2Q}{200 + t} \end{align*}

which gives the equation \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{2}{200 + t}\,Q. \]

Step 4: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\dfrac{2}{200 + t} \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{d}t &= \int \left(-\dfrac{2}{200 + t}\right) \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \,\mathrm{d}Q &= -2\int \dfrac{1}{200 + t} \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= -2(\ln|200 + t|) + C \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= \ln|(200 + t)^{-2}| + C \\[5pt] |Q| &= e^{\ln|(200 + t)^{-2}| + C} \\[5pt] Q(t) &= \dfrac{A}{(200 + t)^2}, \end{align*}

where $A = \pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $180\,\textrm{g}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 180,$ and solve for $A{:}$

\begin{align*} Q(0) &= 180 \\[5pt] \dfrac{A}{(200 + 0)^2} &= 180 \\[5pt] A &= 180(200)^2 \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

\begin{align*} Q(t) &= \dfrac{180(200)^2}{(200 + t)^2} \\[5pt] &= 180\left(\dfrac{200}{200+t}\right)^2 \end{align*}

Now, let $t_o$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $9\,000\,\textrm{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V(t_o) = 9\,000$ to solve for $t_o{:}$

\begin{align*} V(t_o) &= 9\,000 \\[5pt] 30(200+t_o) &= 9\,000 \\[5pt] 200+t_o &= 300 \\[5pt] t_o &= 100\,\textrm{s} \end{align*}

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

\begin{align*} Q(100) &= 180\left(\dfrac{200}{200+100}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= 180\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= 80\,\textrm{g}. \end{align*}

question.text: A tank initially holds $450\,\textrm{gal}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $18\,\textrm{lb}$ of sugar. Fresh water is poured into the tank at a rate of $15\,\textrm{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed sugar solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\textrm{gal/min}.$ Find an equation for the amount of sugar $Q(t),$ in pounds, in the tank $t$ minutes after the fresh water is first added.
question.explanation:
Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} \] describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \]

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{lb}/\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

Step 1: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\textrm{lb/gal}$ of sugar) enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\textrm{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the sugar enters the tank is

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} Q'_{\textrm{in}} &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\dfrac{\textrm{gal}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\cancel{\textrm{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{gal}}}{\textrm{min}}\right)\\[5pt] &= 0\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{min}}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

  • The tank initially contains $450\,\textrm{gal}$ of solution.

  • Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\textrm{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $15t\,\textrm{gal}$ have entered the tank.

  • The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\textrm{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $10t\,\textrm{gal}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is \[ 450 + 15t - 10t = (450+5t)\,\textrm{gal}. \]

Then, since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is \[ \dfrac{Q}{450+5t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{gal}}. \]

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\textrm{gal/min},$ sugar leaves at a rate of \begin{align*} Q'_{\textrm{out}} &= \left(10\,\dfrac{\textrm{gal}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{450+5t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{gal}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(10\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{gal}}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{450+5t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\cancel{\textrm{gal}}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{10Q}{450+5t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{min}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2Q}{90+t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{lb}}{\textrm{min}}. \end{align*}

Step 3: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= 0 - \dfrac{2Q}{90+t} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\dfrac{2}{90+t}\,Q. \end{align*}

Step 4: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\dfrac{2}{90+t} \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{d}t &= \int \left(-\dfrac{2}{90+t}\right) \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \,\mathrm{d}Q &= -2\int \dfrac{1}{90+t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= -2\ln|90+t| + C \\[5pt] |Q| &= e^{-2\ln|90+t| + C} \\[5pt] Q(t) &= \dfrac{A}{(90+t)^2}, \end{align*}

where $A = \pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\textrm{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 18,$ and solve for $A{:}$

\begin{align*} Q(0) &= 18 \\[5pt] \dfrac{A}{(90+0)^2} &= 18 \\[5pt] A &= 18 \cdot 90^2 \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

\[ Q(t) = 18\left(\dfrac{90}{90+t}\right)^2 \]

question.text: A vat initially holds $500\,\textrm{L}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $15\,\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved sugar. Pure water is pumped into the vat at a rate of $14\,\textrm{L/min},$ while the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves the vat at a rate of $10\,\textrm{L/min}.$ Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water pumping begins.
question.explanation:
Let $Q$ be the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t.$ Then, the derivative \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} \] describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \]

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

Step 1: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

Note that pure water (i.e., water containing $0\,\textrm{kg/L}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $14\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the sugar enters the vat is

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} Q'_{\textrm{in}} &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}\right)\cdot \left(14\,\dfrac{\textrm{L}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\cancel{\textrm{L}}}\right)\cdot \left(14\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{L}}}{\textrm{min}}\right)\\[5pt] &= 0\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{min}}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we first determine the volume of solution in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $500\,\textrm{L}$ of solution; water enters at $14\,\textrm{L/min}$ and drains out at $10\,\textrm{L/min}.$ As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ minutes is \[ 500 + 14t - 10t = (500+4t)\,\textrm{L}. \]

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is \[ \dfrac{Q}{500 + 4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}. \]

Therefore, as the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\textrm{L/min},$ sugar leaves at a rate of

\begin{align*} Q'_{\textrm{out}} &= \left(10\,\dfrac{\textrm{L}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{500+4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(10\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{L}}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{500+4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\cancel{\textrm{L}}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{10Q}{500+4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{min}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{min}}. \end{align*}

Step 3: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &=Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \\[5pt] &= 0 - \dfrac{5Q}{2(125+t)} \end{align*} which gives the equation \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{5}{2(125+t)}\,Q. \]

Step 4: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\dfrac{5}{2(125+t)} \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{d}t &= \int \left(-\dfrac{5}{2(125+t)}\right) \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \,\mathrm{d}Q &= -\dfrac{5}{2}\int \dfrac{1}{125+t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= -\dfrac{5}{2}\ln|125+t| + C \\[5pt] |Q| &= e^{-\frac{5}{2}\ln|125+t| + C} \\[5pt] Q(t) &= \dfrac{A}{(125+t)^{5/2}}, \end{align*}

where $A = \pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $15\,\textrm{kg}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 15,$ and solve for $A{:}$

\begin{align*} Q(0) &= 15 \\[5pt] \dfrac{A}{(125+0)^{5/2}} &= 15 \\[5pt] A &= 15\cdot 125^{5/2} \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

\[ Q(t) = 15\left(\dfrac{125}{125+t}\right)^{5/2} \]

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water is first pumped in is

\[ Q(12) = 15\left(\dfrac{125}{139}\right)^{5/2} \approx 11.50\,\textrm{kg}, \]

rounded to two decimal places.

question.text: A $9\,800\,\textrm{mL}$-capacity tank initially holds $7\,000\,\textrm{mL}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $196\,\textrm{g}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $105\,\textrm{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $70\,\textrm{mL/s}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $70\,\textrm{mL/s},$ salt leaves at a rate of \begin{align*} Q'_{\textrm{out}} &= \left(70\,\dfrac{\textrm{mL}}{\textrm{s}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{35(200+t)} \,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{mL}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(70\,\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mL}}}{\textrm{s}}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{35(200+t)} \,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\cancel{\textrm{mL}}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2Q}{200+t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}. \end{align*}

Step 3: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \\[5pt] &= 0 - \dfrac{2Q}{200 + t} \end{align*}

which gives the equation \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{2}{200 + t}\,Q. \]

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\dfrac{2}{200 + t} \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{d}t &= \int \left(-\dfrac{2}{200 + t}\right) \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \cdot \,\mathrm{d}Q &= -2\int \dfrac{1}{200 + t} \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= -2(\ln|200 + t|) + C \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= \ln|(200 + t)^{-2}| + C \\[5pt] |Q| &= e^{\ln|(200 + t)^{-2}| + C} \\[5pt] Q(t) &= \dfrac{A}{(200 + t)^2}, \end{align*}

where $A = \pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.

\begin{align*} Q(0) &= 196 \\[5pt] \dfrac{A}{(200 + 0)^2} &= 196 \\[5pt] A &= 196(200)^2 \end{align*}

\begin{align*} Q(80) &= 196\left(\dfrac{200}{200+80}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= 196\left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)^2 \\[5pt] &= 100\,\textrm{g}. \end{align*}

question.text: A $500\,\textrm{L}$-capacity water tank initially holds $320\,\textrm{L}$ of water containing $20\,\textrm{kg}$ of a dissolved contaminant. Clean water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $9\,\textrm{L/min},$ while the completely mixed water flows out at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$ Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.explanation:
Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative
\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} \] describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \]

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{kg/min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

Step 1: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\textrm{kg/L}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $9\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the contaminant enters the tank is
\begin{align*} \require{cancel} Q'_{\textrm{in}} &= \left(0\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}\right)\cdot \left(9\,\dfrac{\textrm{L}}{\textrm{min}}\right) \\[5pt] &= 0\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{min}}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $320\,\textrm{L}$ of water; clean water enters at $9\,\textrm{L/min},$ and mixed water leaves at $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is
\[ V(t) = 320 + 9t - 5t = (320+4t)\,\textrm{L}. \]

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is
\[ \dfrac{Q}{320+4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}. \]

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min},$ contaminant leaves at a rate of
\begin{align*} Q'_{\textrm{out}} &= \left(5\,\dfrac{\textrm{L}}{\textrm{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\dfrac{Q}{320+4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{L}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5Q}{320+4t}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{min}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5Q}{4(80+t)}\,\dfrac{\textrm{kg}}{\textrm{min}}. \end{align*}

Step 3: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,
\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}} \\[5pt] &= 0 - \dfrac{5Q}{4(80+t)}, \end{align*} which gives
\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{5}{4(80+t)}\,Q. \]

Step 4: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get
\begin{align*} \dfrac1Q \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\dfrac{5}{4(80+t)} \\[5pt] \int \dfrac1Q \,\mathrm{d}Q &= -\dfrac{5}{4}\int \dfrac{1}{80+t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] \ln |Q| &= -\dfrac{5}{4}\ln|80+t| + C. \end{align*}

Thus,
\[ Q(t) = \dfrac{A}{(80+t)^{5/4}}. \]

Using the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$
\begin{align*} \dfrac{A}{80^{5/4}} &= 20 \\[5pt] A &= 20(80)^{5/4}. \end{align*}

So,
\[ Q(t) = 20\left(\dfrac{80}{80+t}\right)^{5/4}. \]

Now, let $t_o$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. Since the tank has a capacity of $500\,\textrm{L},$
\begin{align*} V(t_o) &= 500 \\[5pt] 320+4t_o &= 500 \\[5pt] 4t_o &= 180 \\[5pt] t_o &= 45\,\textrm{min}. \end{align*}

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is
\begin{align*} Q(45) 7 & = 20\left(\dfrac{80}{80+45}\right)^{5/4}\\[5pt] & = 20\left(\dfrac{80}{125}\right)^{5/4}\\[5pt] & \approx 11.45\,\textrm{kg}, \end{align*} rounded to two decimal places.
